title: Evaluate and hand in: your client's feedback, your evaluation, and a final check of your portfolio
kind: an evaluation chapter: it earns AO2 and AO3 marks
one: You ask your client to try your game, and you check your game against each of your requirements. Then you write about your own work, add your code to your portfolio, and check everything before you hand it in.

stages.title: Ask your client, and check your game against your plan

screens.title: Ask your client to try your game, and act on what they say

blocks.p: By the end of this screen, you will have your client's feedback written down, and a change you made because of it.
The marker gives top marks to forms that were improved because a real person tried them. That person is your client.

words: What your client says after trying your game: what works for them and what does not.
Writing how well your game meets each requirement, with evidence for each one.
Something your game cannot do, or does not do well, and how a better version would fix it.
How well you worked: how you used your time, what new skills you learned, and what you would do differently.
A dated list of what you did in each lesson, kept from the start of your project.
Your game's code, copied into your portfolio, with comments that say what each part does.
blocks.intro: You do not need to learn these words now. Where you first meet each one in the chapter, it has a dotted line under it. Hover over it or tap it to see what it means.

blocks.p: Sit with your client while they play your game. Do not help them unless they are stuck.
Write down where they stopped, what they asked, and what they said. That is your [[client feedback|0]].

box.title: An example to read: client feedback on Summit Ready, and the changes it led to

blocks.p: **They said:** "In Listen Out, I clicked a picture before I played the sound, and nothing told me why."
**The change:** the game now says "Play the sound first. You can play it 3 times." The Play button goes grey when it is used up.
**They said:** "In Whiteout, I kept pressing letters I had already tried."
**The change:** each tried letter now turns grey.
Add each change to your storyboard, beside the first drawing, with the reason. The marker looks for changes that were acted on.

screens.title: Evaluate your game against each requirement

blocks.p: By the end of this screen, you will have an [[evaluation|1]] table that checks every requirement from chapter 1.
Start from the evaluation template, so that the table is ready and your time goes on judging your game.

steps.see: Your browser shows that `evaluation-template.docx` has downloaded.
Word shows the evaluation table with its 4 column headings.

img.alt: The evaluation template open in Word, with its 4 column headings and the File menu

marks.say: Click **File**, then **Save As**, and save it in your portfolio folder.

steps.do: Click **File**, then **Save As**, and save it in your portfolio folder.
steps.see: The file name at the top of Word shows the copy in your portfolio folder.

blocks.p: The template holds a table with 4 columns: the requirement, met or partly met or not met, the evidence, and a comment.
The evidence is a test number and a screenshot number from chapter 19, such as T23 and S23.

box.title: An example to read: 3 rows of the Summit Ready evaluation

blocks.p: **R7.** Met. Evidence: T20 to T29, S20 to S29. Every username rule refuses bad data with its own message.
**R11.** Met. Evidence: T33, S33. After 3 wrong tries the button counts down from 30 seconds.
**R15.** Met. Evidence: T60, S60. The sound button turns the sound on and off in every game.
Be honest. A requirement that is partly met, with a clear reason, earns more than one that claims too much.
Go back to your client's words from chapter 1. Write a few sentences on whether your game solves their problem.

screens.title: Write about what your game cannot do

blocks.p: By the end of this screen, you will have written the [[limitations|2]] of your game, and how a better version would fix each one.
Every game has limitations. The marker rewards a pupil who can see them and explain them.
Summit Ready has 2 limitations to read about here. Yours may have the same ones.

code.title: An example to read: a password kept as plain text in players.txt
partLines: The password is there to read
Field 2 is the password, summit42, exactly as the player typed it. Anyone who opens the file can read it.

blocks.p: **Limitation 1: the passwords are kept as plain text.** A real game would store a scrambled version of each password, so nobody could read it from the file.

code.title: An example to read: Sound.cs, which holds one sound player for the whole game
partLines: One player for the whole game
The class is static, which means the game keeps only one copy of it. So there is only one Sound. It holds one SoundPlayer, called player.
A new sound stops the old one
Play gives the one player a new file. A SoundPlayer plays one file at a time, so the old sound stops.

blocks.p: **Limitation 2: only one sound plays at a time.** A new sound stops the one before it. A better version would use a sound library, which is ready-made code that can play two sounds at once.
For each limitation in your game, write what it is, why it matters, and how a better version would fix it.

stages.title: Write about your own work, and add your code

blocks.p: By the end of this screen, you will have written about your [[own performance|3]], using your work log.
The marker wants to read about your time, your skills, and what you would do better next time.
Open your [[work log|4]]. It shows what you did in each lesson, so you can write about your time with real dates.

box.title: Answer these 3 questions in full sentences

blocks.p: **Time:** did you finish each part when you planned to? Which part took longer than you planned, and why?
**Skills:** what can you do now that you could not do at the start? Name each skill, such as writing a class.
**Next time:** what would you do differently, and how would it help?
Give an example for each answer. "I managed my time well" earns little.
"The storyboard took 2 lessons longer than planned, because I redrew the map form" earns more.

screens.title: Add your code to your portfolio, with comments

blocks.p: By the end of this screen, your portfolio will hold a [[code listing|5]] of your game, with a comment on each method.
The marker gives top marks to work that refers to the code in detail. A code listing lets you point to each part.
Look back at Sound.cs on the last screen. Each comment says in one line what the code under it does. Write your comments the same way.

steps.do: In Solution Explorer, double-click one of your own .cs files.
steps.see: The code opens. A green comment line starting with // sits above each method.

img.alt: A form's code in Visual Studio 2019, with a green comment line above each method

marks.say: In Solution Explorer, double-click one of your own .cs files.

steps.do: Click in the code, press Control and A together, then press Control and C together.
steps.see: All the code in the file is copied.

img.alt: The same code in Visual Studio 2019 with every line selected in blue

marks.say: Click in the code, press Control and A together, then press Control and C together.

steps.do: In your Word portfolio, type the file name as a heading, such as frmLogin.cs, then press Control and V together under it.
steps.see: The code sits under its heading, in the same order as in Visual Studio 2019.

img.alt: A Word portfolio page with the heading frmLogin.cs and the code pasted under it

marks.say: In your Word portfolio, type the file name as a heading, such as frmLogin.cs, then press Control and V together under it.

blocks.p: Repeat these 3 steps for each of your own .cs files. Paste only the files you wrote or changed. Leave out the files whose names end in .Designer.cs, which Visual Studio 2019 writes for you.
In your evaluation and your test analysis, name the method that meets each requirement, such as "CheckPasswordsMatch in Player.cs".

stages.title: Check everything, then hand it in

screens.title: The mistakes that cost the most marks

blocks.p: By the end of this screen, you will know the mistakes that cost marks most often, so you can check for each one.
Requirements that no test can check, such as "The game looks good".
A storyboard that shows changes but never says what was done about them.
A test plan that tests all the buttons but only some of the boxes a player types in.
Screenshots of only some forms, or of only some tests.
A screenshot of a message with no sign of the data that caused it.
Saying a requirement is met without pointing to the code that meets it.
A test analysis that lists passes but never says what failed, what was fixed, or what was retested.
An evaluation that does not go back to the requirements from chapter 1, one by one.
Writing about your own performance with no dates, no named skills, and nothing you would change.
A long, untidy portfolio. Short, clear sections in a sensible order earn more than many pages.
Spelling, punctuation and the right technical words count too. Read your portfolio through once, slowly, before you hand it in.

screens.title: Check your portfolio, then hand it in

blocks.p: By the end of this screen, you will have checked every part of your portfolio and handed it in.
Put your portfolio in this order, with a heading for each part: AO1 planning, then AO2 your game and its evidence, then AO3 your evaluation.
Run each check below on your portfolio. Tick each one when it is true.

check.what: Every requirement has a number, and appears in your evaluation table.
check.how: Count the requirements in chapter 1, then count the rows of your evaluation table. The 2 numbers match.

check.what: Every storyboard change says what was changed and why.
check.how: Read each change beside your storyboard. Each one has a reason.

check.what: Every test row has an actual result and a screenshot number that you can find.
check.how: Pick 5 rows. Find each screenshot by its number.

check.what: A row of your evaluation table with no test number and no screenshot number.
check.how: Look at each row. If one has no evidence, find its test and its screenshot, or change it to partly met.
check.fix: Run the test in chapter 19 that shows it, and add the test number and the screenshot number.

check.what: Your client feedback, your limitations, your own performance and your code listing are all there.
check.how: Find the heading for each of the 4 parts.

check.what: Your name is on the first page, and the pages are numbered.
check.how: Look at the first page and the bottom of each page.

blocks.p: Hand in your portfolio and your project folder the way your teacher tells you. Keep your own copy of both.
Your portfolio now holds everything the marker reads: your plan, your game and its evidence, and your evaluation.
Well done. You have built, tested and evaluated a whole game for a real client.
